title: MATH 107: Introduction to Linear Algebra
text:
Welcome
This website contains materials for MATH 107: Introduction to Linear Algebra (3 units, GE Area 2) at Cal Poly Humboldt. Class meets face to face Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, 10:00–10:50 a.m., in FR 201.
Catalog description: Euclidean spaces, matrices and matrix arithmetic, solving systems of equations, and eigenvalues and eigenvectors. Emphasis on applications and use of computation.
This site follows three units: representing and comparing things with vectors; transforming, solving, simulating, and computing with matrices; then explaining dynamics, fitting data, and exploiting structure (eigenvectors, least squares, SVD). Daily learning objectives are on Lectures. Class outlines for later meetings will be posted before those days.

title: MATH 107: Introduction to Linear Algebra
text:
What you’ll learn
By the end of the course you should be able to:

Interpret matrices, vectors, and complex numbers, both algebraically and geometrically.
Solve systems of linear equations using row-reduction techniques by hand and with software.
Find eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a matrix by hand for a \(2\times 2\) matrix and with software for general cases.
Understand and apply eigenvalues and eigenvectors to solve problems.
Recognize special types of matrices and their properties, such as triangular, symmetric, and positive definite matrices.
Communicate in the language of linear algebra, including linear combination, subspace, span, independence, basis, and dimension.
Write or adapt programs to implement linear algebra concepts, such as matrix arithmetic, vectors, and plotting.
Apply linear algebra to real-world problems.
Learn independently as well as collaboratively. Develop study techniques that include pre- and post-reading of class materials and be able to critically analyze and implement solutions in a team setting.

title: Lecture 10 — Clustering and \(k\)-means
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Explain the goal of clustering.
Compute one assignment/update iteration of \(k\)-means.
Interpret a centroid as a vector.
Recognize that clustering output depends on representation, scaling, and initialization.

title: Lecture 10 — Clustering and \(k\)-means
text:
Warm-up
Six points in \(\mathbb{R}^2\): \[
(0,0),\ (0,1),\ (1,0),\quad (5,5),\ (5,6),\ (6,5).
\] By eye, into how many natural groups do they fall? Suggest a representative (center) for each group.

title: Lecture 10 — Clustering and \(k\)-means
text:
Fill in
Clustering partitions \(N\) vectors \(x_1,\ldots,x_N\) into \(k\) groups so that vectors in the same group are \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) to each other (small pairwise distances).
A group representative (centroid, when we use the mean) \(z_j\) is a vector that stands for cluster \(j\). The basic clustering objective sums squared distances from each point to its group’s representative: \[
J^{\mathrm{clust}} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \lVert x_i - z_{c_i}\rVert^2,
\] where \(c_i\) is the cluster index of \(x_i\).
\(k\)-means alternates two steps:

Assignment: given representatives \(z_1,\ldots,z_k\), set each \(c_i\) to the index of the \(\underline{\hspace{2.8cm}}\) \(z_j\) to \(x_i\).
Update: given assignments, replace each \(z_j\) by the \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) of the points currently in cluster \(j\).

The algorithm is a \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\): different initial \(z_j\) can yield different final clusterings. Feature \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) and the choice of \(k\) also change the result.

title: Lecture 10 — Clustering and \(k\)-means
text:
Worked in class
W1. Goal in words. A café has purchase vectors (coffee, tea, pastry counts) for many customers. What would clustering these vectors help the café do?
W2. One assignment step. Data: \[
x_1=(0,0),\ x_2=(0,2),\ x_3=(8,0),\ x_4=(8,2).
\] Representatives \(z_1=(1,1)\), \(z_2=(7,1)\). Assign each \(x_i\) to the nearest \(z_j\). List the two clusters.
W3. One update step. Using your clusters from W2, replace each \(z_j\) by the mean of its points. What are the new centroids?
W4. Interpret a centroid. If a cluster of temperature vectors has centroid \((54,53,55)\) for three morning hours, what does that vector mean?
W5. Sensitivity. Same four points as W2, but start with \(z_1=(0,1)\), \(z_2=(0,0)\). After one assignment, what goes wrong if both points near the origin grab almost everything? (One sentence on initialization.)

title: Lecture 10 — Clustering and \(k\)-means
text:
Check yourself
C1. In \(k\)-means assignment, each point is assigned by a \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) computation to the current representatives.
C2. For points \((0,0),(2,0)\) in one cluster, the centroid is \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\).
C3. True or false: running \(k\)-means once always finds the global minimum of \(J^{\mathrm{clust}}\).
C4. Why might you standardize features before clustering customer data that mixes age and annual spending?
C5. If \(k=N\) (one cluster per point), what is \(J^{\mathrm{clust}}\) after a perfect fit of representatives?






NoteAnswers (Check yourself only)





C1. nearest-neighbor (distance to each representative)
C2. \((1,0)\)
C3. False. It is a heuristic; different initializations can give different local solutions.
C4. So spending in dollars does not dominate age in years inside Euclidean distance.
C5. \(J^{\mathrm{clust}}=0\) (each point is its own representative).

title: Lecture 14 — Basis, dimension, and orthonormal vectors
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Explain what a basis accomplishes.
Identify a basis and dimension in simple examples.
Use linear combination, span, subspace, independence, basis, and dimension accurately.
Recognize an orthonormal collection.
Explain why orthonormal coordinates are convenient for measurement and reconstruction.

title: Lecture 14 — Basis, dimension, and orthonormal vectors
text:
Warm-up
Let \(a=(1,0)\) and \(b=(1,1)\).

Is \(\{a,b\}\) independent? Does it span \(\mathbb{R}^2\)?
Can every \(v=(v_1,v_2)\) be written uniquely as \(\alpha a+\beta b\)? (Try \(v=(2,3)\).)

title: Lecture 14 — Basis, dimension, and orthonormal vectors
text:
Fill in
A basis of a subspace \(V\) is a list of vectors that is both

\(\underline{\hspace{2.8cm}}\) (no redundancy), and
a \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) set for \(V\) (every vector in \(V\) is a linear combination of the list).

What a basis accomplishes: every \(v\in V\) has coefficients (coordinates) with respect to the basis — a unique recipe \(v=\beta_1 a_1+\cdots+\beta_k a_k\).
The dimension of \(V\) is the number of vectors in \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) of \(V\). (All bases of \(V\) have the same length.)
Examples:

\(\dim\mathbb{R}^n=\underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}\) (standard basis \(e_1,\ldots,e_n\)).
A line through the origin through a nonzero \(a\) has dimension \(\underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}\).
A plane through the origin spanned by two independent vectors has dimension \(\underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}\).

An orthonormal list \(q_1,\ldots,q_k\) satisfies \(q_i^{\mathsf{T}}q_j=\underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}\) if \(i\neq j\), and \(\lVert q_i\rVert=\underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}\).
For an orthonormal basis of a subspace, the coefficients of \(v\) are especially simple: \[
\beta_i = \underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}
\] (inner products — no linear system to solve). That is why orthonormal coordinates are convenient for measurement and reconstruction.

title: Lecture 14 — Basis, dimension, and orthonormal vectors
text:
Worked in class
W1. Basis or not? For each list, is it a basis of \(\mathbb{R}^2\)? If not, say whether it fails independence, spanning, or both.

\((1,0),\ (0,1)\)
\((1,1),\ (2,2)\)
\((1,0),\ (0,1),\ (1,1)\)
\((1,1)\) alone

W2. Dimension. Let \(V=\operatorname{span}\{(1,2,0),(2,4,0),(0,0,1)\}\). Find a basis of \(V\) and \(\dim V\).
W3. Vocabulary drill. Fill each blank with one of: linear combination, span, subspace, independent, dependent, basis, dimension.

\(\operatorname{span}\{a,b\}\) is always a \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) of \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
If \(c=2a-b\), then \(\{a,b,c\}\) is \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\).
A \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) of \(V\) is an independent spanning list for \(V\).

W4. Orthonormal check. Which of these pairs in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) is orthonormal?

\((1,0),\ (0,1)\)
\((1,1)/\sqrt{2},\ (1,-1)/\sqrt{2}\)
\((1,0),\ (1,1)\)

W5. Orthonormal coordinates. Let \(q_1=(1,0)\) and \(q_2=(0,1)\) (standard basis — already orthonormal). For \(v=(3,-2)\), what are \(\beta_1=q_1^{\mathsf{T}}v\) and \(\beta_2=q_2^{\mathsf{T}}v\)? Check \(v=\beta_1 q_1+\beta_2 q_2\).
W6 (time permitting). Gram–Schmidt idea. From independent \(a_1=(1,1)\) and \(a_2=(1,0)\), form \(q_1=a_1/\lVert a_1\rVert\), then subtract from \(a_2\) its projection onto \(q_1\), and normalize. (Board sketch only.)

title: Lecture 14 — Basis, dimension, and orthonormal vectors
text:
Check yourself
C1. A basis of a subspace is a list that is \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) and \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\).
C2. \(\dim\operatorname{span}\{(1,0,0),(0,1,0)\}=\underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}\).
C3. True or false: every spanning list for \(V\) is a basis of \(V\).
C4. If \(\{q_1,q_2\}\) is orthonormal and \(v=\beta_1 q_1+\beta_2 q_2\), then \(\beta_1=\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\).
C5. Why are orthonormal coordinates nicer than coordinates in a skewed basis like \((1,0),\ (1,1)\)?






NoteAnswers (Check yourself only)





C1. independent and spanning (for that subspace).
C2. \(2\)
C3. False. Spanning lists can be dependent (too many vectors); a basis cannot.
C4. \(\beta_1=q_1^{\mathsf{T}}v\)
C5. Coefficients are inner products (no \(2\times 2\) solve); lengths and angles stay easy because the basis vectors are unit and orthogonal.

title: Lecture 20 — Transforming space
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Predict the effect of scaling, reflection, shear, and rotation matrices.
Apply matrices to many 2D or 3D points at once.
Plot and compare original and transformed objects.
Adapt a short program that implements a transformation.
Interpret a matrix as a coordinate or physical-space transformation.

title: Lecture 20 — Transforming space
text:
Warm-up
Predict, without multiplying: where does \(A=\operatorname{diag}(2,1/2)\) send the point \((1,1)\)? Sketch the original and image roughly.

title: Lecture 20 — Transforming space
text:
Fill in
Many geometric maps on \(\mathbb{R}^2\) (or \(\mathbb{R}^3\)) are matrix-vector products \(y=Ax\).
Finding the matrix. The \(j\)th column of \(A\) is what the map does to \(\underline{\hspace{1.2cm}}\). So apply the geometry to \(e_1,e_2\) (and \(e_3\) in 3D) to read off columns.
Common \(2\times 2\) examples:

Scaling / dilation: \(A=\operatorname{diag}(s_1,s_2)\) stretches the axes by \(s_1,s_2\).
Rotation counterclockwise by \(\theta\): \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\ \sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Reflection through a line through the origin; shear (e.g. \(\begin{bmatrix}1&k\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\)).

Many points at once. If columns of \(X\) are points, then \(AX\) applies the same map to every column.
Change of coordinates (3D idea). Body-fixed vs earth-fixed frames: \(x_{\mathrm{earth}}=p+Qx_{\mathrm{body}}\), where columns of \(Q\) are the body axes expressed in earth coordinates.

title: Lecture 20 — Transforming space
text:
Worked in class
W1. Build from \(e_1,e_2\). Reflection through the \(x_1\)-axis sends \((1,0)\mapsto(1,0)\) and \((0,1)\mapsto(0,-1)\). Write \(A\). Check \(A(2,3)\).
W2. Rotation. For \(\theta=90^\circ=\pi/2\), write the rotation matrix and compute \(A(1,0)\) and \(A(0,1)\). Does that match “\(90^\circ\) counterclockwise”?
W3. Many points. Let \(X=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&1\\0&1&1\end{bmatrix}\) (three corners of a right triangle). With \(A=\operatorname{diag}(2,1)\), compute \(AX\) and describe the image.
W4 (time permitting). Shear \(A=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\). Where do \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\) go? Sketch the unit square’s image.

title: Lecture 20 — Transforming space
text:
Your turn
Y1. Reflection through the \(x_2\)-axis: write \(A\) by tracking \(e_1\) and \(e_2\), then compute \(A(3,-1)\).
Y2. Rotation by \(180^\circ\): write \(A\) and apply it to \((2,1)\).
Y3. True or false: every \(2\times 2\) matrix represents a rotation of the plane.






NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. \(e_1\mapsto(-1,0)\), \(e_2\mapsto(0,1)\), so \(A=\begin{bmatrix}-1&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\). \(A(3,-1)=(-3,-1)\).
Y2. \(A=\begin{bmatrix}-1&0\\0&-1\end{bmatrix}=-I\). \(A(2,1)=(-2,-1)\).
Y3. False. Scaling, shear, projections, and many other maps are also \(2\times 2\) matrices; rotations are a special family.

title: Lecture 23 — RREF, pivots, free variables, and software
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Interpret reduced row echelon form.
Identify pivot and free variables.
Describe a solution set parametrically.
Distinguish inconsistent, unique, and infinite-solution cases.
Use software to solve or row-reduce a system and verify the answer using a residual.

title: Lecture 23 — RREF, pivots, free variables, and software
text:
Warm-up
The RREF of an augmented matrix is \[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 & 2 & | & 3 \\
0 & 1 & -1 & | & 4 \\
0 & 0 & 0 & | & 0
\end{bmatrix}.
\] Which variables are pivots? Which are free? Write the general solution.

title: Lecture 23 — RREF, pivots, free variables, and software
text:
Fill in
Reduced row echelon form (RREF) is echelon form with these extras:

Each pivot is \(\underline{\hspace{0.8cm}}\).
Each pivot is the \(\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\) nonzero in its column (zeros above and below).

A pivot variable (basic variable) corresponds to a pivot column. A free variable has \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) pivot in its column; assign a parameter (e.g. \(x_3=t\)).
Reading the RREF of \([A\mid b]\):







Pattern
Conclusion




A row \([0\ \cdots\ 0\mid c]\) with \(c\neq 0\)
\(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\)


Every column of \(A\) has a pivot, and consistent
\(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) solution


Consistent, and at least one free variable
\(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) solutions



Software. Use a solver or RREF command (Octave rref, Python SymPy rref, or a course helper). Always verify a candidate \(x\) by computing the residual \(Ax-b\) (should be near \(\underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}\)).

title: Lecture 23 — RREF, pivots, free variables, and software
text:
Worked in class
W1. Classify from RREF (no original system needed).

\[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 & | & 2 \\
0 & 1 & | & -1
\end{bmatrix}
\]
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 2 & | & 3 \\
0 & 0 & | & 1
\end{bmatrix}
\]
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 2 & 0 & | & 1 \\
0 & 0 & 1 & | & 4
\end{bmatrix}
\]

W2. Parametric form. From \[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 3 & 0 & | & 2 \\
0 & 0 & 1 & | & -1
\end{bmatrix},
\] identify free variable(s) and write \(x=(x_1,x_2,x_3)\) in terms of parameter(s).
W3. Software + residual. For \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{bmatrix},\quad
b=\begin{bmatrix}5\\11\end{bmatrix},
\] solve \(Ax=b\) with Octave or Python. Compute \(Ax-b\) and confirm it is (numerically) zero.
Octave sketch: A\[b] or rref([A b]) then read \(x\).
Python sketch: np.linalg.solve(A,b) for square invertible \(A\), or SymPy Matrix.hstack(A,b).rref().
W4. Inconsistent check. Invent a \(2\times 2\) augmented RREF that is inconsistent. What would \(Ax-b\) look like if software “forced” a least-squares answer? (One sentence — foreshadow Week 15.)

title: Lecture 23 — RREF, pivots, free variables, and software
text:
Your turn
Y1. From RREF \[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 & -2 & | & 5 \\
0 & 1 & 3 & | & -1 \\
0 & 0 & 0 & | & 0
\end{bmatrix},
\] list pivot variables, free variables, and the general solution.
Y2. True or false: if RREF has a row of all zeros including the augmented entry, the system is inconsistent.
Y3. You solve \(Ax=b\) in software and get \(x=(1,-1)\). You compute \(Ax-b=(0.0,\,10^{-15})\). Was the solve successful? Why check the residual?
Y4. A \(3\times 5\) matrix \(A\) (after RREF of \([A\mid b]\), consistent) has \(3\) pivots. How many free variables? Unique solution or infinitely many?






NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. Pivot variables \(x_1,x_2\); free \(x_3=t\). Then \(x_1-2t=5\) and \(x_2+3t=-1\), so \[
x=(5+2t,\,-1-3t,\,t),\quad t\in\mathbb{R}.
\]
Y2. False. A zero row including the right-hand side is consistent (redundant equation). Inconsistency needs \([0\ \cdots\ 0\mid c]\) with \(c\neq 0\).
Y3. Yes — residual is numerically zero (roundoff). Checking \(Ax-b\) catches wrong \(x\), singular/ill-conditioned cases, and copy-paste mistakes.
Y4. \(n=5\) unknowns and \(3\) pivots \(\Rightarrow\) \(2\) free variables \(\Rightarrow\) infinitely many solutions (when consistent).

title: Lecture 29 — Same mathematics, very different computational cost
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Compare algebraically equivalent orders of computation.
Count intermediate values that must be stored.
Measure runtime for increasing problem sizes.
Explain why forming a large intermediate matrix may be wasteful.
Choose a computational order and justify it quantitatively.

title: Lecture 29 — Same mathematics, very different computational cost
text:
Warm-up
Let \(a=(1,2)\), \(b=(3,4)\), \(c=(1,-1)\) (column vectors).

Form the outer product \(ab^{\mathsf{T}}\) (a \(2\times 2\) matrix).
Compute \((ab^{\mathsf{T}})c\) and \(a(b^{\mathsf{T}}c)\). Same vector?

title: Lecture 29 — Same mathematics, very different computational cost
text:
Fill in
Associativity. For compatible sizes, \((XY)z=X(Yz)\). In particular, for \(n\)-vectors \(a,b,c\), \[
(ab^{\mathsf{T}})c = a(b^{\mathsf{T}}c).
\] Same mathematical result — different \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\).
Order 1 — form the matrix first. Compute \(M=ab^{\mathsf{T}}\) (\(n\times n\)), then \(Mc\).

Intermediate storage: about \(\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\) numbers (the whole matrix \(M\)).
Cost idea: building \(M\) and multiplying by \(c\) scales like \(\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\) work (order \(n^2\)).

Order 2 — scalar first. Compute \(s=b^{\mathsf{T}}c\) (one number), then \(sa\).

Intermediate storage: the scalar \(s\), plus the vectors — order \(\underline{\hspace{1.2cm}}\) numbers, not \(n^2\).
Cost idea: two inner/scale passes — order \(\underline{\hspace{1.2cm}}\) work.

Why wasteful? Forming \(ab^{\mathsf{T}}\) materializes a dense \(n\times n\) matrix you may never need as an object; then you immediately collapse it with \(c\). Capstone theme: choose an algorithm that matches the structure, not only the formula on the page.
Runtime. In software you can time both orders for growing \(n\) and justify which order to use with measured times (and storage counts).

title: Lecture 29 — Same mathematics, very different computational cost
text:
Worked in class
W1. Algebra. With \(a=(2,0,-1)\), \(b=(1,1,1)\), \(c=(1,0,1)\), compute \(s=b^{\mathsf{T}}c\) and \(a(b^{\mathsf{T}}c)\). Then form \(ab^{\mathsf{T}}\) and \((ab^{\mathsf{T}})c\). Match?
W2. Storage count. For general \(n\), how many entries does \(ab^{\mathsf{T}}\) have? How many numbers do you store for the scalar-first method beyond the three input vectors?
W3. Choose an order. You need \(y=(ab^{\mathsf{T}})c\) for \(n=5000\) once. Which order do you run, and what two quantitative reasons (storage + flops/runtime idea) support the choice?
W4 (preview). Sketch what a timing table should look like: rows \(n=200,1000,3000\); columns “form \(ab^{\mathsf{T}}\) then multiply” vs “scalar first.” What qualitative pattern do you expect?

title: Lecture 29 — Same mathematics, very different computational cost
text:
Your turn
Y1. Let \(a=(1,-1,0)\), \(b=(2,1,3)\), \(c=(0,1,1)\). Compute both \((ab^{\mathsf{T}})c\) and \(a(b^{\mathsf{T}}c)\).
Y2. For \(n=100\), about how many intermediate entries does Order 1 store in \(ab^{\mathsf{T}}\)? Order 2 in the scalar \(s\)?
Y3. One sentence: why can two algebraically equal expressions have wildly different runtimes?






NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. \(b^{\mathsf{T}}c=2\cdot 0+1\cdot 1+3\cdot 1=4\), so \(a(b^{\mathsf{T}}c)=4a=(4,-4,0)\). The matrix route gives the same: \[
ab^{\mathsf{T}}=\begin{bmatrix}2&1&3\\-2&-1&-3\\0&0&0\end{bmatrix},\qquad
(ab^{\mathsf{T}})c=(4,-4,0).
\]
Y2. Order 1 stores \(n^2=10{,}000\) entries in \(ab^{\mathsf{T}}\). Order 2 stores one scalar \(s\) as the essential intermediate (beyond the inputs).
Y3. Associativity preserves the value but not the work: different parenthesizations create different intermediates (e.g. an \(n\times n\) matrix vs a scalar), so flops and memory — and therefore runtime — can differ by orders of magnitude.

Learning objectives

Recognize the determinant of a triangular matrix from its diagonal.

title: Lecture 32 — Determinants, geometry, and invertibility
text:
Warm-up
Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\0&3\end{bmatrix},\qquad
B=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{bmatrix}.
\]

What does \(x\mapsto Ax\) do to the unit square? What is the area of the image?
Are the columns of \(B\) independent? Guess whether \(B\) is invertible.

title: Lecture 32 — Determinants, geometry, and invertibility
text:
Fill in
For \(A=\begin{bmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{bmatrix}\), \[
\det A = ad-bc.
\] Geometrically, \(|\det A|\) is the \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) scaling factor of the unit square under \(x\mapsto Ax\) (signed area encodes orientation).
Triangular / diagonal. If \(T\) is upper or lower triangular (including diagonal), \[
\det T = \underline{\hspace{3.2cm}}.
\]
Invertibility. For square \(A\): \[
A\text{ invertible}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \det A \neq \underline{\hspace{0.8cm}}.
\] If \(\det A=0\), the image of the unit cube/square is \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) (lost dimension): columns are dependent, \(Ax=b\) fails for some \(b\), and \(N(A)\) is nontrivial.
Product rule (preview). \(\det(AB)=(\det A)(\det B)\). Useful later for compositions.
Coming attraction. Eigenvalues solve \(\det(A-\lambda I)=0\) — the characteristic equation. Today’s \(\det\) is the tool; Week 13 builds the theory.

title: Lecture 32 — Determinants, geometry, and invertibility
text:
Worked in class
W1. Compute.

\(\det\begin{bmatrix}3&1\\0&2\end{bmatrix}\)
\(\det\begin{bmatrix}1&4&0\\0&-2&5\\0&0&3\end{bmatrix}\)
\(\det\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\4&2\end{bmatrix}\)

W2. Area scaling. Let \(A=\begin{bmatrix}0&-2\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\). Compute \(\det A\). Where do \(e_1\) and \(e_2\) go? What area does the unit square map to?
W3. Zero determinant. Explain, in one sentence each, why \(\det\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{bmatrix}=0\) means (i) noninvertible and (ii) the image of the unit square has area zero.
W4. Link to Monday. For invertible \(2\times 2\) \(A\), the formula for \(A^{-1}\) has \(\det A\) in the denominator. What goes wrong if \(\det A=0\)?
W5. Characteristic preview. For \(A=\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\0&3\end{bmatrix}\), expand \(\det(A-\lambda I)\) as a quadratic in \(\lambda\). (No need to “solve eigenvalues” yet — just form the polynomial.)

title: Lecture 32 — Determinants, geometry, and invertibility
text:
Your turn
Y1. Compute \(\det\begin{bmatrix}4&-1\\2&3\end{bmatrix}\) and \(\det\begin{bmatrix}-1&0&0\\2&5&0\\3&1&2\end{bmatrix}\).
Y2. Let \(A=\operatorname{diag}(2,-1)\). What is \(|\det A|\)? Interpret as area scaling of the unit square.
Y3. True or false: if \(\det A=0\) for square \(A\), then \(Ax=b\) has either no solution or infinitely many solutions for every \(b\).






NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. \(\det\begin{bmatrix}4&-1\\2&3\end{bmatrix}=12-(-2)=14\). Lower triangular: \(\det=(-1)(5)(2)=-10\).
Y2. \(|\det A|=|(2)(-1)|=2\): the unit square is mapped to a rectangle of area \(2\) (stretched by \(2\) horizontally and reflected/flipped vertically).
Y3. True. Singular means no unique solution for any \(b\): if \(b\in C(A)\) there are infinitely many solutions; otherwise none.

title: Lecture 37 — Why did the system behave that way?
text:
Warm-up
Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1.1&0.2\\0.1&0.8\end{bmatrix},\qquad
v=\begin{bmatrix}2\\1\end{bmatrix}.
\] Hand-compute \(Av\). Guess a plausible \(\lambda\) so that \(Av\approx\lambda v\). (Exact eigenpairs come from software in lab.)

title: Lecture 37 — Why did the system behave that way?
text:
Fill in
Software eigenpairs. Octave eig(A) / Python np.linalg.eig(A) return eigenvalues and a matrix whose columns are eigenvectors.
Verify. For each reported pair \((\lambda,v)\), check \[
Av \approx \underline{\hspace{1.4cm}}
\] (componentwise; floating-point noise is expected). Never trust a bare printout without this check.
Dominant behavior. If \(|\lambda_1|>|\lambda_2|\ge\cdots\) and \(x_0\) has a component along the \(\lambda_1\)-eigenvector, then for large \(t\) \[
A^t x_0 \approx c\,\lambda_1^t\,v_1.
\] That explains Lab 4-style growth/decay/stabilization once you know the eigenpairs.
Complex eigenvalues. For a real matrix, nonreal eigenvalues come in conjugate pairs. In the real plane they produce \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) (rotation / oscillation), matching Monday’s pure-rotation example.
Normal modes (demo, not a DE course). For a symmetric mass–spring style matrix, eigenvectors are often \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) (orthogonal). Software shows the modes; we do not derive differential equations today.

title: Lecture 37 — Why did the system behave that way?
text:
Worked in class
W1. Software sketch. On the board / laptop, for \(A=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}\):
# Octave:  [V,D] = eig(A)     or    eig(A)
# Python:  vals, vecs = np.linalg.eig(A)
Read off \(\lambda\)’s and columns of \(V\). Verify \(A v_1=\lambda_1 v_1\) for one column.
W2. Explain a simulation. Same \(A\) as W1; \(x_0=(1,0)\). Using eigenpairs, explain in one sentence why \(x_t\) grows and which direction it approaches.
W3. Complex / oscillation. Software on \(R=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\) should report eigenvalues near \(\pm i\). Connect that to the cycling you saw in Lab 4 stretch / Lecture 35.
W4. Symmetric demo. Let \(S=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}\) (symmetric). Check that the two eigenvectors from W1 are orthogonal (\(v_1^{\mathsf{T}}v_2=0\)). Normal-mode pictures use the same idea in higher dimension.

title: Lecture 37 — Why did the system behave that way?
text:
Your turn
Y1. Pseudocode: given \(A\), obtain eigenpairs in software and write the one-line check that \(Av\approx\lambda v\) for the first pair.
Y2. True or false: if \(|\lambda_1|=1.5\) and \(|\lambda_2|=0.5\), then for generic \(x_0\) the long-run direction of \(A^t x_0\) is the \(\lambda_1\)-eigendirection.






NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. Sample: vals, V = np.linalg.eig(A) then A @ V[:,0] - vals[0]*V[:,0] (should be near \(0\)); Octave: [V,D]=eig(A) then A*V(:,1) - D(1,1)*V(:,1).
Y2. True. The \(\lambda_1\) term grows relative to \(\lambda_2\), so the state aligns with \(v_1\) (unless the \(v_1\)-component of \(x_0\) is exactly zero).

title: Lecture 38 — When \(Ax=b\) has no exact solution
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Recognize an inconsistent overdetermined system.
Formulate the least-squares objective \(\min_x \lVert Ax-b\rVert\).
Interpret the fitted vector as the closest attainable vector.
Interpret the residual geometrically.
Distinguish an exact solution from a best approximate solution.

title: Lecture 38 — When \(Ax=b\) has no exact solution
text:
Warm-up
Consider the overdetermined system \(Ax=b\) with \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\1&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix},\qquad
b=\begin{bmatrix}1\\2\\2\end{bmatrix}.
\]

How many equations? How many unknowns? Is \(A\) tall, wide, or square?
Suppose someone guesses \(x=(1,0.5)\). Compute \(Ax\) and \(Ax-b\). Is \(x\) an exact solution?

title: Lecture 38 — When \(Ax=b\) has no exact solution
text:
Fill in
Overdetermined / inconsistent. When there are more independent equations than unknowns, \(Ax=b\) often has \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) exact solution. The right-hand side \(b\) may lie outside the column space \(C(A)\).
Least-squares idea. Instead of insisting on \(Ax=b\), choose \(\hat{x}\) to make \(A\hat{x}\) as close as possible to \(b\): \[
\hat{x}\;=\;\arg\min_x\;\lVert Ax-b\rVert.
\] The vector \(\hat{b}=A\hat{x}\) is the \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) attainable right-hand side in \(C(A)\).
Residual. The residual is \[
r = b - A\hat{x}
\] (some texts write \(A\hat{x}-b\); same length \(\|r\|\)). Geometrically, \(r\) is the leftover after projecting \(b\) onto \(C(A)\) — it is orthogonal to every column of \(A\) at a minimizer (Wednesday).
Exact vs approximate.







Situation
Meaning




Exact solution
\(Ax=b\) for some \(x\) \(\Leftrightarrow\) \(b\in\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\)


Least-squares solution
minimizes \(\|Ax-b\|\); residual may be \(\underline{\hspace{1.2cm}}\)



If an exact solution exists, it is also a least-squares solution (residual zero).

title: Lecture 38 — When \(Ax=b\) has no exact solution
text:
Worked in class
W1. Inconsistent check. For the warm-up \(A\) and \(b\), argue that no \(x=(x_1,x_2)\) can satisfy all three equations simultaneously. (Hint: equations 1–2 force \(x_2=1\); plug into equation 3.)
W2. Objective value. With the same \(A,b\) and trial \(x=(1,0.5)\), compute \(\|Ax-b\|\) (Euclidean). Is this the minimum? (You need not prove optimality yet — just evaluate the objective.)
W3. Closest attainable vector. Sketch (in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) as a cartoon, or think in words): \(C(A)\) is a plane (or line) through the origin; \(b\) is off the plane; \(\hat{b}=A\hat{x}\) is the foot of the perpendicular from \(b\) to \(C(A)\). Label the residual \(r=b-\hat{b}\).
W4. Exact case. Change \(b\) to \(b'=(1,2,3)\). Show that \(x=(1,1)\) solves \(Ax=b'\) exactly. What is the residual? What is \(\min_x\|Ax-b'\|\)?
W5. Language check. In one sentence each, distinguish “no solution” from “best approximate solution.”

title: Lecture 38 — When \(Ax=b\) has no exact solution
text:
Your turn
Y1. Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\0&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix},\qquad
b=\begin{bmatrix}3\\1\\1\end{bmatrix},\qquad
x=\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix}.
\] Compute \(Ax\) and \(r=b-Ax\). Is \(x\) an exact solution? What is \(\|r\|\)?
Y2. True or false, with a one-line reason: if \(Ax=b\) is inconsistent, then no vector \(\hat{x}\) can make \(\|A\hat{x}-b\|\) finite.
Y3. In words: what does \(\hat{b}=A\hat{x}\) represent when \(\hat{x}\) is a least-squares solution?
Y4. A \(4\times 2\) matrix \(A\) has linearly independent columns, and \(b\notin C(A)\). Can \(Ax=b\) have an exact solution? Can it have a least-squares solution?






NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. \(Ax=(2,1,1)\); \(r=(1,0,0)\); not exact. \(\|r\|=1\).
Y2. False. The residual norm is always finite; least squares still chooses an \(\hat{x}\) that minimizes it (even when the minimum is positive).
Y3. \(\hat{b}\) is the closest vector in the column space \(C(A)\) to the observed \(b\) — the attainable right-hand side under the model \(Ax\).
Y4. Exact: no (\(b\notin C(A)\)). Least squares: yes (minimizer of \(\|Ax-b\|\) still exists; uniqueness follows from independent columns).

text:
Learning objectives
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Plot observed and fitted values.
Interpret residuals and an RMS error in context.
Check the residual’s orthogonality to the columns of \(A\).
Evaluate whether a fitted model is useful rather than merely reporting coefficients.
Recognize that \(A^{\mathsf{T}}A\) is symmetric positive semidefinite, explain \(x^{\mathsf{T}}A^{\mathsf{T}}Ax=\lVert Ax\rVert^2\), and recognize that \(A^{\mathsf{T}}A\) is positive definite when \(A\) has linearly independent columns.

title: Lecture 39 — Least squares, data fitting, and positive definiteness
text:
Warm-up
Monday’s setup: minimize \(\|Ax-b\|\). At a minimizer \(\hat{x}\), the residual \(r=b-A\hat{x}\) is orthogonal to \(C(A)\), which is equivalent to the normal equations \[
A^{\mathsf{T}}A\,\hat{x}=A^{\mathsf{T}}b.
\]

If \(A\) is \(m\times n\) with \(m>n\), what size is \(A^{\mathsf{T}}A\)? Why is that nicer than solving \(Ax=b\) directly?
True or false: \(A^{\mathsf{T}}A\) is always symmetric.

title: Lecture 39 — Least squares, data fitting, and positive definiteness
text:
Fill in
Normal equations / software. Solving \(A^{\mathsf{T}}A\hat{x}=A^{\mathsf{T}}b\) (when \(A\) has independent columns) gives the unique least-squares \(\hat{x}\). In practice we often call a solver instead of forming \(A^{\mathsf{T}}A\) by hand:








Task
Octave
Python




Least-squares \(\hat{x}\)
xhat = A \ b
xhat = np.linalg.lstsq(A, b, rcond=None)[0]


Fitted values
bhat = A*xhat
bhat = A @ xhat


Residual
r = b - bhat
r = b - bhat


RMS
rms = norm(r)/sqrt(m)
rms = np.linalg.norm(r)/np.sqrt(m)



Orthogonality check. At a least-squares solution, \(A^{\mathsf{T}}r \approx \underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}\) (numerical noise ok).
RMS. Root-mean-square residual \(\mathrm{RMS}=\|r\|/\sqrt{m}\) reports a typical per-equation error in the same units as \(b\).
Useful vs coefficients. Always ask: do fitted values track the data? Is RMS small in context? Blindly quoting \(\hat{x}\) is not enough.
Positive semidefinite / definite (Boyd / class notes). A symmetric matrix \(P\) is positive semidefinite (PSD) if \(x^{\mathsf{T}}Px\ge 0\) for all \(x\); positive definite (PD) if \(x^{\mathsf{T}}Px>0\) for all \(x\neq 0\).
For any \(A\): \[
x^{\mathsf{T}}(A^{\mathsf{T}}A)x = \lVert Ax\rVert^2 \ge 0,
\] so \(A^{\mathsf{T}}A\) is always \(\underline{\hspace{2.8cm}}\). It is positive definite precisely when \(Ax=0\Rightarrow x=0\), i.e. when \(A\) has \(\underline{\hspace{2.8cm}}\) columns — then the normal equations have a unique solution.

title: Lecture 39 — Least squares, data fitting, and positive definiteness
text:
Worked in class
W1. Tiny fit by hand / software. Four campus shuttle wait times (minutes) at hours \(t=1,2,3,4\) after 8am: \[
b=(6,\,7,\,10,\,11).
\] Model a line \(b\approx x_1 + x_2 t\) with \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}
1&1\\1&2\\1&3\\1&4
\end{bmatrix}.
\]

Form \(A^{\mathsf{T}}A\) and \(A^{\mathsf{T}}b\) (or use A\b / lstsq).
Report \(\hat{x}=(x_1,x_2)\) and the fitted values \(\hat{b}=A\hat{x}\).
Compute \(r\) and RMS. In one sentence: is a linear trend reasonable here?

Expected (for checking): \(\hat{x}=(4,\,1.8)\) exactly from the normal equations; \(\hat{b}=(5.8,\,7.6,\,9.4,\,11.2)\); RMS \(=\sqrt{0.2}\approx 0.45\) minutes.
W2. Orthogonality. With your \(\hat{x}\) from W1, compute \(A^{\mathsf{T}}r\). Should it be near \((0,0)\)?
W3. Plot story. On axes “hour \(t\)” vs “wait (min)”, sketch data points and the fitted line. Where is the residual for \(t=1\) visible?
W4. PSD identity. Expand \(x^{\mathsf{T}}A^{\mathsf{T}}Ax\) for \(A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\1&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}\) and a general \(x=(x_1,x_2)\). Confirm it equals \(\|Ax\|^2\) and is \(\ge 0\).
W5. PD vs PSD. Explain why \(A^{\mathsf{T}}A\) fails to be positive definite if the two columns of \(A\) are equal. What goes wrong for uniqueness of \(\hat{x}\)?

title: Lecture 39 — Least squares, data fitting, and positive definiteness
text:
Your turn
Y1. Using the W1 data, suppose software returns \(\hat{x}=(4,\,1.8)\). Compute \(\hat{b}_1=x_1+x_2\cdot 1\) and the first residual \(r_1=b_1-\hat{b}_1\).
Y2. True or false: \(A^{\mathsf{T}}A\) is always positive definite for every \(A\).
Y3. Why check \(A^{\mathsf{T}}r\approx 0\) after a least-squares solve?
Y4. A fit has RMS \(=0.02\) °C for outdoor temperature data that typically varies by \(10\) °C across the day. Useful model, or not? One sentence.






NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. \(\hat{b}_1=4+1.8=5.8\); \(r_1=6-5.8=0.2\).
Y2. False. \(A^{\mathsf{T}}A\) is always PSD, but PD only when \(A\) has linearly independent columns (equivalently \(\ker A=\{0\}\)).
Y3. It is the normal-equation / geometric check that the residual is orthogonal to \(C(A)\) — evidence that \(\hat{x}\) really is a least-squares critical point (up to roundoff).
Y4. Useful in context: RMS \(\ll\) the natural scale of the data, so typical pointwise error is tiny compared with day-scale variation.

title: Lecture 40 — SVD and capstone launch
text:
Warm-up (after quiz)
A grayscale image (or one video frame) is an \(m\times n\) matrix of pixel intensities.

Roughly how many numbers store the full matrix?
If most “information” lived in a few patterns, why might a factored low-rank form save storage?

title: Lecture 40 — SVD and capstone launch
text:
Fill in
SVD (conceptual). Every real \(m\times n\) matrix factors as \[
A = U\Sigma V^{\mathsf{T}},
\] where the columns of \(U\) and \(V\) are orthonormal (left / right singular vectors) and \(\Sigma\) is rectangular “diagonal” with nonnegative singular values \[
\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\cdots\ge 0
\] on its main diagonal. Think: \(A\) = rotate/reflect → stretch by \(\sigma_i\) → rotate/reflect.
Rank-\(k\) approximation. Keep the largest \(k\) singular values (and matching singular-vector columns); set the rest to zero. The truncated product \[
A_k = U_k\Sigma_k V_k^{\mathsf{T}}
\] is the best rank-\(k\) approximation in the usual 2-norm / Frobenius sense (details in the slides / capstone).
Software sketch (capstone / later):








Task
Octave
Python




SVD
[U,S,V] = svd(A)
U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(A, full_matrices=False)


Rank-\(k\) rebuild
use first \(k\) columns / \(\sigma\)’s
U[:,:k] @ np.diag(S[:k]) @ Vt[:k,:]



Capstone launch (one question). For a short clip of frames: when is it better to compress each frame alone versus encode \(F_1\) and differences \(D_2=F_2-F_1\), \(D_3=F_3-F_2\)? Trade off accuracy, storage, runtime, and resource use — including the cost of computing the SVD itself. Full prompts live in the capstone packet; studio is Mon Dec 7.

title: Lecture 40 — SVD and capstone launch
text:
Worked in class (short)
W1. Read \(\Sigma\). Suppose a \(4\times 3\) matrix has singular values \(\sigma=(10,\,2,\,0.1)\). What is \(\operatorname{rank}(A)\) (numerically “full” vs tiny)? For a rank-\(1\) approximation, which \(\sigma\) do you keep?
W2. Storage cartoon. Full \(m\times n\) needs \(mn\) entries. A rank-\(k\) factorization stores about \(k(m+n+1)\) numbers (columns of \(U_k\), \(V_k\), and \(k\) singular values). When is \(k(m+n+1)\ll mn\)?
W3. Frames vs differences (launch). Three frames \(F_1,F_2,F_3\). Plan A: compress each. Plan B: compress \(F_1\), \(D_2=F_2-F_1\), \(D_3=F_3-F_2\). In one sentence each: when might Plan B win on storage? What must you still check (error / runtime)?

title: Lecture 40 — SVD and capstone launch
text:
Your turn
Y1. In \(A=U\Sigma V^{\mathsf{T}}\), what do the singular values measure conceptually (one phrase)?
Y2. True or false: computing an SVD is always “free,” so low-rank multiplication is always faster overall.
Y3. Write one capstone question you care about (accuracy, storage, runtime, or resource use) for frames vs frame-differences. One sentence is enough — expand in studio.






NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. Stretch factors / importance of each singular-vector mode (how strongly \(A\) amplifies that direction).
Y2. False. The factorization itself can be expensive; low-rank reuse only pays off when approximation quality is good and you reuse the factors enough (see capstone notes).
Y3. Any clear tradeoff question is fine — e.g. “For my three frames, does difference encoding cut storage at the same relative error, after counting SVD time?”

Course Description (Catalog Description)
Euclidean spaces, matrices and matrix arithmetic, solving systems of equations, and eigenvalues and eigenvectors. Emphasis on applications and use of computation.
Division: Lower Division.
Weekly: Lecture 3 hrs.
Instruction Mode: Face to face only.
Prerequisite: (MATH 101 and MATH 101T) or MATH 102 or ALEKS PPL assessment score 78–100 or appropriate high school coursework. All prerequisite courses must be passed with a grade of C− or higher. See Math Placement and ALEKS PPL for details.
Note: if you plan to use MATH 107 as a prerequisite for another MATH, DATA, or STAT course, you must have a grade of C− or better in this course.

Course Learning Outcomes
By the end of this course, students will be able to:

Interpret matrices, vectors, and complex numbers, both algebraically and geometrically.
Solve systems of linear equations using row-reduction techniques by hand and with software.
Find eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a matrix by hand for a \(2\times 2\) matrix and with software for general cases.
Understand and apply eigenvalues and eigenvectors to solve problems.
Recognize special types of matrices and their properties, such as triangular, symmetric, and positive definite matrices.
Communicate in the language of linear algebra, including linear combination, subspace, span, independence, basis, and dimension.
Write or adapt programs to implement linear algebra concepts, such as matrix arithmetic, vectors, and plotting.
Apply linear algebra to real-world problems.
Learn independently as well as collaboratively. Develop study techniques that include pre- and post-reading of class materials and be able to critically analyze and implement solutions in a team setting.

Daily learning objectives for each meeting are on Lectures.


General Education & Institutional Learning Outcomes
This course fulfills Lower Division General Education Area 2 (Mathematics) and supports Cal Poly Humboldt’s Institutional Learning Outcomes related to quantitative reasoning, critical thinking, and communication.

The policies for late or missed work are as follows:

Lecture attendance is required, but I know that sometimes you will need to miss class due to illness or other emergencies. Each student may miss up to 10 lecture days without penalty and without contacting me. Reserve these days for emergencies. Mon Oct 19 — Linear dynamical systems
Lecture 24 page
Reading: Boyd 9.1–9.3
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Represent an evolving system as \(x_{t+1}=Ax_t\).
Interpret the state vector and transition matrix.
Build a transition matrix from a flow description.
Compute and interpret the next few states.

title: Lectures
section: Wed Oct 21 — Simulation and long-run behavior
text:
Wed Oct 21 — Simulation and long-run behavior
Lecture 25 page
Reading: Simulation of linear dynamics
Watch for long-run patterns; the eigenvalue explanation comes in Week 13.
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Simulate many time steps computationally.
Plot state components through time.
Recognize stabilization, growth, decay, or oscillation.
Conduct a simple what-if simulation.
State limitations of a linear dynamical model.

title: Lectures
section: Fri Oct 23 — Predict a system through time + Quiz 7 + Lab 2
text:
Fri Oct 23 — Predict a system through time + Quiz 7 + Lab 2
Lecture 26 page · Quiz 7 · Lab 2
Reading: Lachniet Ch. 2 (matrix operations) and Lachniet’s introductory programming/loops material; Lab 2.
Quiz 7 is Week 8 (systems / RREF), not Lab 2 and not today’s dynamics lecture. Graded dynamics practice is Lab 4 on November 6.
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Implement a linear dynamical model.
Write or complete a short iterative calculation.
Validate the first steps by hand.
Compare results under altered parameters or initial states.
Record an unexplained long-run pattern for later investigation.

title: Lectures
text:
Mon Oct 26 — Matrix multiplication
Lecture 27 page
Reading: Boyd 10.1
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Determine whether a product is defined and give its dimensions.
Compute a small matrix product.
Interpret \(ABx\) as a sequence of transformations.
Explain why matrix multiplication is generally not commutative.

title: Lectures
section: Wed Oct 28 — Composition and matrix powers
text:
Wed Oct 28 — Composition and matrix powers
Lecture 28 page
Reading: Boyd 10.2–10.3
Connect matrix powers to the dynamics you simulated in Week 9.
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Combine multistage processes using a matrix product.
Connect \(A^k x\) to repeated dynamics.
Interpret selected entries of a matrix product or power.
Recognize how network and transition information accumulates through powers.

title: Lectures
section: Fri Oct 30 — Same mathematics, very different computational cost + Quiz 8 + Lab 3
text:
Fri Oct 30 — Same mathematics, very different computational cost + Quiz 8 + Lab 3
Lecture 29 page · Quiz 8 · Lab 3
Reading: Boyd’s \(ab^{\mathsf{T}}c\) example; Lab 3.
Quiz 8 is Week 9 dynamics, not today’s cost lecture and not Lab 3. Order-of-computation ideas return in the capstone.
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Compare algebraically equivalent orders of computation.
Count intermediate values that must be stored.
Measure runtime for increasing problem sizes.
Explain why forming a large intermediate matrix may be wasteful.
Choose a computational order and justify it quantitatively.

title: Lectures
text:
Mon Nov 2 — Inverses and solving
Lecture 30 page
Reading: Boyd 11.1–11.3
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Interpret an inverse as undoing a transformation.
Determine whether a simple matrix is invertible.
Connect invertibility to uniqueness of \(Ax=b\).
Explain why solving \(Ax=b\) is generally preferable computationally to explicitly calculating \(A^{-1}\).

title: Lectures
section: Wed Nov 4 — Rank, column space, null space, and basis connections
text:
Wed Nov 4 — Rank, column space, null space, and basis connections
Lecture 31 page
Reading: Boyd plus selected portions of Strang §3.5, especially rank, column space, null space, basis, and dimension.
Not a full four-subspaces theory unit. Row space and left nullspace are enrichment, not quiz material.
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Interpret column space and null space through \(Ax=b\) and \(Ax=0\).
Determine rank from pivots or independent columns.
Find simple bases for column or null spaces.
Connect rank to consistency, independence, and dimension.
Use subspace, basis, dimension, rank, column space, and null space correctly.

title: Lectures
section: Fri Nov 6 — Determinants, geometry, and invertibility + Quiz 9 + Lab 4
text:
Fri Nov 6 — Determinants, geometry, and invertibility + Quiz 9 + Lab 4
Lecture 32 page · Quiz 9 · Lab 4
Reading: Determinants (class notes); Lab 4.
Quiz 9 is Week 10 (products / powers / cost), not today’s determinants and not Lab 4.
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Compute determinants of \(2\times 2\) and simple triangular matrices.
Interpret determinant magnitude as area or volume scaling.
Connect determinant zero with lost dimension and noninvertibility.
Recognize the determinant of a triangular matrix from its diagonal.
Connect determinants to the coming characteristic equation.

title: Lectures
section: Mon Nov 16 — Eigenvectors as persistent directions
text:
Mon Nov 16 — Eigenvectors as persistent directions
Lecture 35 page
Reading: Beginning of Strang §6.1 — \(Ax=\lambda x\), eigenvectors, and dynamics.
Start with the unexplained behavior from Lab 4. The free PDF is only §6.1.
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Explain geometrically what makes \(v\) an eigenvector.
Verify a proposed eigenpair.
Find \(\lambda\) when an eigenvector is given.
Connect eigenvectors to repeated transformations and steady directions.
Recognize that a rotation may have no real eigenvector, motivating complex numbers.

title: Lectures
section: Wed Nov 18 — Characteristic equation, \(2\times 2\) eigenproblems, and complex numbers
text:
Wed Nov 18 — Characteristic equation, \(2\times 2\) eigenproblems, and complex numbers
Lecture 36 page
Reading: Strang §6.1, characteristic equation and the complex-eigenvalue (\(90^\circ\) rotation) example.
Meets the explicit hand-calculation and complex-number CLOs. The same free §6.1 file is used Nov 16–20.
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Interpret \(a+bi\) algebraically and as a point/vector in the complex plane.
Perform the basic complex arithmetic needed for eigenvalue calculations.
Form and solve \(\det(A-\lambda I)=0\) for a \(2\times 2\) matrix.
Find corresponding eigenvectors.
Check real or complex eigenpairs by substitution.

title: Lectures
section: Fri Nov 20 — Why did the system behave that way? + Quiz 10 + Lab 5
text:
Fri Nov 20 — Why did the system behave that way? + Quiz 10 + Lab 5
Lecture 37 page · Quiz 10 · Lab 5
Reading: Strang §6.1, Lab 5, and Lachniet Ch. 5 (eigenvalues/eigenvectors).
Normal modes appear as an application demo (not a differential-equations course). Quiz 10 is Week 11 (inverses / rank / determinants), not today’s eigen lab.
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Compute eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a general matrix with software.
Verify \(Av\approx\lambda v\) numerically.
Use dominant eigenbehavior to explain a simulated system.
Interpret complex eigenvalues as rotation/oscillation behavior.
Explore a symmetric-matrix or normal-mode example and observe orthogonal eigenvectors.

title: Lectures
section: Mon Nov 30 — When \(Ax=b\) has no exact solution
text:
Mon Nov 30 — When \(Ax=b\) has no exact solution
Lecture 38 page
Reading: Boyd 12.1
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Recognize an inconsistent overdetermined system.
Formulate the least-squares objective \(\min_x \lVert Ax-b\rVert\).
Interpret the fitted vector as the closest attainable vector.
Interpret the residual geometrically.
Distinguish an exact solution from a best approximate solution.

title: Lectures
section: Wed Dec 2 — Least squares, data fitting, and positive definiteness
text:
Wed Dec 2 — Least squares, data fitting, and positive definiteness
Lecture 39 page
Reading: Boyd 12.2–12.4 and 13.1, class notes on symmetric and positive-definite matrices, and Lachniet Ch. 2 (least-squares / data-fitting exercises).
Positive definiteness is from Boyd and class notes. Software practice is Lab 6 on Friday; Quiz 11 is Week 13 (eigenvalues), not least squares.
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Compute a least-squares solution with Octave or Python.
Plot observed and fitted values.
Interpret residuals and an RMS error in context.
Check the residual’s orthogonality to the columns of \(A\).
Evaluate whether a fitted model is useful rather than merely reporting coefficients.
Recognize that \(A^{\mathsf{T}}A\) is symmetric positive semidefinite, explain \(x^{\mathsf{T}}A^{\mathsf{T}}Ax=\lVert Ax\rVert^2\), and recognize that \(A^{\mathsf{T}}A\) is positive definite when \(A\) has linearly independent columns.

title: Lectures
section: Fri Dec 4 — SVD, Lab 6, Quiz 11, and capstone launch
text:
Fri Dec 4 — SVD, Lab 6, Quiz 11, and capstone launch
Lecture 40 page · Lab 6 · Quiz 11
Reading: Selected slides from the Strang/MIT SVD slides (not all 17 pages), Lab 6, capstone launch, Lachniet Ch. 5 (SVD) and Ch. 7 (image compression).
Quiz 11 is Week 13 eigenvalues, not today’s SVD or Lab 6. SVD and capstone launch share the period with Lab 6.
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Interpret \(A=U\Sigma V^{\mathsf{T}}\) conceptually.
Construct a rank-\(k\) approximation computationally.
Compare singular-value decay for an image/frame and a frame-difference matrix.
Encode three frames either independently or as \(F_1\), \(D_2\), \(D_3\).
Compare reconstruction error and storage for the two approaches.
Formulate a capstone question involving accuracy, storage, runtime, and resource use.

Reading: Capstone (no new mathematics)
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Implement and validate a low-rank computational strategy.
Measure approximation error, storage, and runtime.
Separate one-time factorization cost from repeated-use cost.
Compare theoretical operation/storage counts with empirical measurements.
Debug and refine an analysis collaboratively while retaining individual understanding.

text:
Wed Dec 9 — Capstone presentations / gallery walk
Lecture 42 page
Reading: Capstone presentations
Pair lightning talks or gallery walk.
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Explain the problem and why SVD or another linear-algebra tool was appropriate.
Present quantitative evidence about accuracy and cost.
Defend a choice of rank or representation.
Evaluate classmates’ methods constructively.
Communicate the practical value and limitations of the result.

Fri Dec 11 — Cumulative final review

Connect vectors, systems, transformations, dynamics, eigenvectors, least squares, and SVD.
Select an appropriate method for a new situation.

If you choose Python, use Google Colab for lab work (hosted Jupyter; no local install). Exercises appear on each lab hub next to the Octave versions.

Beginner guide; later, linear algebra

Introductory guide



Polars is for real tables: reading files, selecting columns, filtering, transforming, and handing numerical columns to NumPy. NumPy is for arrays, indexing, and later solve, eig, lstsq, svd, norms, and determinants. Plotnine is for scatterplots, line plots, fitted relationships, residual plots, clustering graphics, and other standard figures; it uses a grammar-of-graphics syntax and works directly with Polars DataFrames.
As with Lachniet, these pages support syntax. The lab hub and in-class one-pager are the assigned work.
